{"answer": "# Cryogenic mechanical testing of metals: equipment and facilities

**The operating distinction is the specimen environment, not merely the refrigerator rating.** Liquid-nitrogen immersion provides approximately 77 K; liquid-helium immersion provides approximately 4.2 K. Tests near 20 K can instead use temperature-controlled helium gas or direct liquid-hydrogen immersion. A Gifford–McMahon (GM) or pulse-tube cold head rated near 4 K does **not** establish that a loaded metal specimen reaches or remains at 4 K. The cited cryogen-free metal tests demonstrate approximately 20 K; the documented 4 K bulk-metal tension, fatigue and fracture tests principally use liquid helium. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000036)

The following comparison separates measured operation from proposed capability. Its cited studies and DOIs are discussed below. (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000039)

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

## Cooling arrangements and mechanical measurements

**Immersion cryostats.** A servo-hydraulic or electrodynamic frame applies force through long, aligned pull rods and grips inside a vacuum-insulated dewar. For 77 K tests, specimens and grips are submerged in LN₂; for 4 K tests, systems commonly pre-cool with LN₂, remove it and fill with LHe. ISO 6892-4 and ASTM E1450 describe immersed-helium tensile practice: keep the specimen submerged, use displacement control and limit the nominal strain rate to approximately 10⁻³ s⁻¹ or below. Immersion supplies strong thermal coupling, particularly useful during plastic deformation and prolonged fatigue, but demands cryogen transfers, level monitoring and oxygen-deficiency precautions. NIST’s published protocol used a minimum five-minute immersion soak and independently calibrated its clip gages in each liquid. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000035)

**Controlled gas and flow-through chambers.** For a selected temperature between bath boiling points, gas can be cooled by passing liquid cryogen through a heat exchanger or by expanding/vaporizing it into an insulated specimen enclosure; a sensor near the specimen, flow control and a heater establish the setpoint. This is *not equivalent* to immersing the specimen. At NASA Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC), liquid helium entered distributed, orificed tubes in an insulated fatigue-crack-growth chamber and had vaporized before leaving them: the specimen experienced **cold gaseous He at −423 °F, approximately 20 K**, not an LHe bath at 4 K. Thermocouples on both specimen faces and in the chamber monitored a reported +5/−10 °F temperature band. The rig required continuous operator monitoring and a 5,000-US-gallon helium tanker for the extended tests; that tanker capacity is **not** the amount consumed per test. KIT describes a distinct, two-chamber LN₂/LHe transfer-cooled arrangement in which the specimen is *not immersed*, specifically avoiding liquid-bubble interference with extensometer signals. (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000035)

**Liquid hydrogen.** MSFC’s Hydrogen Test Facility used a dedicated cryostat with automatic LH₂ filling to keep Inconel 718 crack-growth specimens completely submerged at −423 °F. Tests at 20 Hz followed ASTM E647; front-face clip-gage compliance tracked crack length, checked against optical measurements after testing. Direct LH₂ testing tests both **temperature and hydrogen exposure**, whereas helium gas at the same temperature is an inert thermal surrogate. In that particular alloy/test series, LH₂ and cold-He crack-growth results broadly agreed, but LH₂ testing was expensive enough that an additional desired near-threshold test was not undertaken. The source is Wells, Wright and Hastings, *NASA/TM-2005-213948* (2005); **no DOI was identified**. Precharging a specimen with hydrogen and subsequently testing it in inert helium at 20 or 4 K is likewise not testing *in* liquid hydrogen. (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000042)

**Cryogen-free, conduction-cooled rigs.** A vacuum jacket and multilayer-insulated radiation shield intercept room-temperature heat; the first cryocooler stage cools the shield, while a copper bridge or strap connects the colder stage to a specimen vessel or grips. Some designs add a small sealed charge of high-purity **helium exchange gas** to couple the specimen thermally: *no liquid helium* does not mean *no helium gas*. Thermometers must characterize the loaded specimen or its immediate fixture, since load-train conduction, contact resistance and deformation heating can leave it considerably warmer than the second-stage cold head. A Chinese two-GM system achieved a **16.8 K specimen** after about eight hours, with up to 0.3 K spatial variation, and tested Ti–6Al–4V at 20 K through quartz windows using digital image correlation (DIC). A Korean ULVAC UHE15 GM system, whose second stage is *rated* at 1.5 W at 4.2 K, took about 13 hours to reach a **20 K specimen** and reported approximately ±0.3 K control around it. The Korean studies performed metal tension and ASTM E1820 compact-specimen, unloading-compliance J-integral fracture testing, rather than demonstrating 4 K specimen tests. DOIs: [10.1088/1757-899X/278/1/012083](https://doi.org/10.1088/1757-899X/278/1/012083), [10.3390/pr10112401](https://doi.org/10.3390/pr10112401), [10.3390/met13101774](https://doi.org/10.3390/met13101774). (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000041)

**Pulse tubes:** Washington State University’s HYPER laboratory couples a **Cryomech PT-415** to an MTS Acumen 12 inside a vacuum-insulated rig, using a copper thermal strap and hydrogen liquefaction for about 20 K testing; its reported demonstrations concern **polymer composites**, although its authors say appropriately small specimens of some metals could fit. It reports up to 100 Hz fatigue capability, not a demonstrated 100 Hz metal test at 4 K. A separate Toulouse/Laboratoire National des Champs Magnétiques Intenses (LNCMI) pulse-tube installation uses a copper vessel and He exchange gas, reaches 20 K in about three hours and warms in about 4.5 hours; the reported tests are also **composites**. Its stated ability to cool to 4 K should not be cited as a demonstrated *4 K metal-test temperature*. DOI for CRAFT: [10.1088/1757-899X/1240/1/012080](https://doi.org/10.1088/1757-899X/1240/1/012080); no DOI was identified for the LNCMI abstract. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000039)

## Where the documented capabilities are

- **NIST, United States:** an MTS 55-kip (about 222 kN) servo-hydraulic frame, 100 kN load cell and three Shepic clip gages measured welded-316L tension at **77 K in LN₂ and 4 K in LHe**; the same report situates these measurements within an ASME–NASA–NIST fracture-toughness programme. It specifies three tensile specimens per weld at 77 K and two per weld at 4 K—not an annual throughput figure. DOI: [10.6028/NIST.TN.2229](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.TN.2229). (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032)
- **National High Magnetic Field Laboratory, Tallahassee:** LHe-immersed, typically **100 kN servo-hydraulic** systems perform **4 K tension, compact-tension fatigue-crack growth and J-integral fracture toughness** of magnet steels; the methods invoke ASTM E1450, E647 and E1820. DOI: [10.1088/1757-899X/279/1/012001](https://doi.org/10.1088/1757-899X/279/1/012001). (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000023)
- **NIMS and its predecessor National Research Institute for Metals, Tsukuba:** published titanium-alloy high-cycle fatigue tests used **LN₂ at 77 K and a recondensing LHe bath at 4 K**, with a ±100 kN dynamic-capacity servo-hydraulic machine; frequencies were reduced to limit specimen heating. The predecessor’s closed-loop helium-recondensing fatigue plant demonstrated **more than 460 hours** of continuous operation. DOIs: [10.1016/j.cryogenics.2005.10.011](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cryogenics.2005.10.011), [10.2355/isijinternational1966.26.48](https://doi.org/10.2355/isijinternational1966.26.48). (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030)
- **CERN Mechanical and Materials Engineering, Geneva:** four earlier **18 kN** sub-size cryostats were supplemented by an in-house **100 kN, 300–4 K** immersion cryostat for standard-size metallic tensile specimens. The 2015 account demonstrates 4 K results but presents low-temperature fracture work as an intended future use of the adaptable frame, **not** as a fracture programme demonstrated in that paper. DOI: [10.1088/1757-899X/102/1/012007](https://doi.org/10.1088/1757-899X/102/1/012007). (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000040)
- **KIT CryoMaK, Karlsruhe:** published facility ranges are **MTS 25, room temperature–7 K; MTS 50, room temperature–77 K; MTS 100, ATLAS and PHOENIX, room temperature–4.2 K**; listed facilities support combinations of tension, fatigue, fracture toughness and component testing. Its MTS 100 Landmark is rated **100 kN, up to 40 Hz**. The report described integration of that particular new cryostat as planned for 2016, so the table of facility capabilities should not be read as proof that *every* newly listed configuration was commissioned in 2015. DOI: [10.12776/ams.v21i4.650](https://doi.org/10.12776/ams.v21i4.650). (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000018)
- **NASA MSFC, Alabama:** the Hydrogen Test Facility demonstrated direct **20 K LH₂** metal crack-growth tests; a separate continuous-flow cold-He chamber produced **20 K** inert comparison tests. **NASA Glenn, Ohio:** its later cryogen-free **LESTR** uses an Instron ElectroPuls E10000 and a Sumitomo closed-cycle cooler for **40–125 K metal-wire** tension and bend/fatigue work—not 20 K or 4 K. DOI for LESTR: [10.64631/lhoi2310](https://doi.org/10.64631/lhoi2310); MSFC report: *NASA/TM-2005-213948*, no DOI identified. (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000045, pqac-00000048)
- **UK National Physical Laboratory:** its published **250 kN, ambient-to-4 K** static/dynamic mechanical cryostat is a **capability design/requirements study**, including controlled intermediate temperatures, not evidence in that report of commissioned metal tests. DOI: [10.47120/npl.mat102](https://doi.org/10.47120/npl.mat102). (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007)

## Strain, crack-opening and temperature instrumentation

Direct cryogenic strain measurement is preferred to inferring specimen strain from actuator travel, which includes load-train compliance and thermal contraction. Reported implementations include NIST’s **three Shepic ball-ended clip gages** on 25.4 mm-gage rings, calibrated separately at 77 and 4 K; NHMFL’s **Shepic clip-on extensometers** for tension and clip-on crack-opening-displacement (COD) gages for compact specimens; CERN’s **CEME C-shaped 50 mm and W-shaped 25 mm extensometers**, calibrated at room temperature, 77 and 4 K; and **Epsilon Model 3442, 10 mm** gages in the Korean 20 K studies. KIT describes in-house clip-on instruments with **350 Ω strain-gage Wheatstone bridges** and temperature-dependent calibration. Fracture tests additionally require measured load-line displacement/COD and validated crack-length tracking, particularly where discontinuous yielding upsets unloading compliance. (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000040)

Bonded cryogenic strain gages need temperature-dependent gage-factor and thermal-output correction; opposed gages can help diagnose bending, and the load train must be checked for axial alignment. Optical DIC avoids mounting a contact extensometer on the specimen but requires insulated windows and a stable speckle image; the Chinese study explicitly compared 20 K DIC with two Epsilon extensometers. A cold-stage reading alone is insufficient during serrated yielding or cyclic heating: NIMS measured internal specimen temperature rise with an embedded thermocouple, and the Korean investigators deliberately slowed tension to **5 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹** in their 304L study. (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000040)

**Commercial equipment actually named in methods** includes MTS and Instron frames; **Walter + bai** 100 kN-static/80 kN-dynamic frames; **SUNS PLS 100**; **ULVAC UHE15** GM, **Cryomech PT-415** pulse-tube and **Sumitomo CH-110LT** cryocoolers; **Epsilon**, **Shepic** and CEME-developed extensometers; and **Lake Shore Model 335** temperature control. CERN’s 100 kN cryostat and KIT’s described cryogenic hardware are institutionally built/integrated; the cited studies do not establish a commercial maker for those cryostats. KIT also lists Galdabini and INSTRON CEAST impact machines, but those should **not** be mislabelled as its 4 K fatigue frames. (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000048)

## Helium, time and cost: what is actually reported

CERN calculated **25–30 L of LHe for one test** in its approximately **15 L** cryostat, with **20–25 minutes of cooldown between tests** at the specified filling pressure; this is a turnaround component, not the duration of every test. The NIMS predecessor reported about **50 L LHe and 300 kg LN₂ at startup**, approximately **15 kg LN₂ per hour** for shielding, and roughly **15 L LHe added after exchanging a specimen**, while requiring **no added LHe during uninterrupted recondensing operation**. Its optimized initial closure took about **six hours**, exchange/reclosure about **two hours**, and continuous operation exceeded **460 hours**. These figures describe different accounting boundaries and must not be compared as though all were LHe *per specimen*. (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000034)

NPL’s **25–30 L LHe during an optimized 30-minute cooldown** is a *design estimate* for a proposed roughly 20–25 L dewar, not a measured cost or consumption per completed test. GM-cooled metal rigs avoid LHe purchases but reported **8–13-hour cooldowns** and still use small amounts of exchange He gas, electricity and cryocooler infrastructure. LH₂ requires dedicated storage, venting, detection and safety systems; MSFC explicitly notes the expense of additional LH₂ tests. The retrieved primary studies provide **no comparable currency-denominated capital price, helium price per litre, or fully burdened cost per metal specimen**; deriving one without local supply, recovery, labour and duty-cycle data would be misleading. (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000041)"}

CERN calculated **25–30 L of LHe for one test** in its approximately **15 L** cryostat, with **20–25 minutes of cooldown between tests** at the specified filling pressure; this is a turnaround component, not the duration of every test. LH₂ requires dedicated storage, venting, detection and safety systems; MSFC explicitly notes the expense of additional LH₂ tests. The retrieved primary studies provide **no comparable currency-denominated capital price, helium price per litre, or fully burdened cost per metal specimen**; deriving one without local supply, recovery, labour and duty-cycle data would be misleading. # Cryogenic mechanical testing of metals: equipment and facilities

**The operating distinction is the specimen environment, not merely the refrigerator rating.** Liquid-nitrogen immersion provides approximately 77 K; liquid-helium immersion provides approximately 4.2 K. Tests near 20 K can instead use temperature-controlled helium gas or direct liquid-hydrogen immersion. A Gifford–McMahon (GM) or pulse-tube cold head rated near 4 K does **not** establish that a loaded metal specimen reaches or remains at 4 K. **Immersion cryostats.** A servo-hydraulic or electrodynamic frame applies force through long, aligned pull rods and grips inside a vacuum-insulated dewar. For 77 K tests, specimens and grips are submerged in LN₂; for 4 K tests, systems commonly pre-cool with LN₂, remove it and fill with LHe. ISO 6892-4 and ASTM E1450 describe immersed-helium tensile practice: keep the specimen submerged, use displacement control and limit the nominal strain rate to approximately 10⁻³ s⁻¹ or below. Immersion supplies strong thermal coupling, particularly useful during plastic deformation and prolonged fatigue, but demands cryogen transfers, level monitoring and oxygen-deficiency precautions. NIST’s published protocol used a minimum five-minute immersion soak and independently calibrated its clip gages in each liquid. (perez2022mechanicaltestingof pages 12-15, perez2022mechanicaltestingof pages 15-18, weeks2022tensiletestsat pages 8-12, perez2022mechanicaltestingof pages 21-23)

**Controlled gas and flow-through chambers.** For a selected temperature between bath boiling points, gas can be cooled by passing liquid cryogen through a heat exchanger or by expanding/vaporizing it into an insulated specimen enclosure; a sensor near the specimen, flow control and a heater establish the setpoint. This is *not equivalent* to immersing the specimen. At NASA Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC), liquid helium entered distributed, orificed tubes in an insulated fatigue-crack-growth chamber and had vaporized before leaving them: the specimen experienced **cold gaseous He at −423 °F, approximately 20 K**, not an LHe bath at 4 K. Thermocouples on both specimen faces and in the chamber monitored a reported +5/−10 °F temperature band. The rig required continuous operator monitoring and a 5,000-US-gallon helium tanker for the extended tests; that tanker capacity is **not** the amount consumed per test. KIT describes a distinct, two-chamber LN₂/LHe transfer-cooled arrangement in which the specimen is *not immersed*, specifically avoiding liquid-bubble interference with extensometer signals. (sas2015cryomak–theoverviewof pages 3-8, wells2005fatiguecrackgrowth pages 6-9, perez2022mechanicaltestingof pages 21-23)

**Liquid hydrogen.** MSFC’s Hydrogen Test Facility used a dedicated cryostat with automatic LH₂ filling to keep Inconel 718 crack-growth specimens completely submerged at −423 °F. Tests at 20 Hz followed ASTM E647; front-face clip-gage compliance tracked crack length, checked against optical measurements after testing. Direct LH₂ testing tests both **temperature and hydrogen exposure**, whereas helium gas at the same temperature is an inert thermal surrogate. In that particular alloy/test series, LH₂ and cold-He crack-growth results broadly agreed, but LH₂ testing was expensive enough that an additional desired near-threshold test was not undertaken. The source is Wells, Wright and Hastings, *NASA/TM-2005-213948* (2005); **no DOI was identified**. Precharging a specimen with hydrogen and subsequently testing it in inert helium at 20 or 4 K is likewise not testing *in* liquid hydrogen. (wells2005fatiguecrackgrowth pages 6-9, wells2005fatiguecrackgrowth pages 9-13, kim2022metallicmaterialevaluation pages 2-4, damm2025hydrogen–dislocationinteractionsat pages 4-7)

**Cryogen-free, conduction-cooled rigs.** A vacuum jacket and multilayer-insulated radiation shield intercept room-temperature heat; the first cryocooler stage cools the shield, while a copper bridge or strap connects the colder stage to a specimen vessel or grips. Some designs add a small sealed charge of high-purity **helium exchange gas** to couple the specimen thermally: *no liquid helium* does not mean *no helium gas*. Thermometers must characterize the loaded specimen or its immediate fixture, since load-train conduction, contact resistance and deformation heating can leave it considerably warmer than the second-stage cold head. A Chinese two-GM system achieved a **16.8 K specimen** after about eight hours, with up to 0.3 K spatial variation, and tested Ti–6Al–4V at 20 K through quartz windows using digital image correlation (DIC). A Korean ULVAC UHE15 GM system, whose second stage is *rated* at 1.5 W at 4.2 K, took about 13 hours to reach a **20 K specimen** and reported approximately ±0.3 K control around it. **Pulse tubes:** Washington State University’s HYPER laboratory couples a **Cryomech PT-415** to an MTS Acumen 12 inside a vacuum-insulated rig, using a copper thermal strap and hydrogen liquefaction for about 20 K testing; its reported demonstrations concern **polymer composites**, although its authors say appropriately small specimens of some metals could fit. # Cryogenic mechanical testing of metals: equipment and facilities

**The operating distinction is the specimen environment, not merely the refrigerator rating.** Liquid-nitrogen immersion provides approximately 77 K; liquid-helium immersion provides approximately 4.2 K. Tests near 20 K can instead use temperature-controlled helium gas or direct liquid-hydrogen immersion. A Gifford–McMahon (GM) or pulse-tube cold head rated near 4 K does **not** establish that a loaded metal specimen reaches or remains at 4 K. The cited cryogen-free metal tests demonstrate approximately 20 K; the documented 4 K bulk-metal tension, fatigue and fracture tests principally use liquid helium. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000036)

The following comparison separates measured operation from proposed capability. Its cited studies and DOIs are discussed below. (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000039)

*Table: Comparison of demonstrated and proposed cryogenic mechanical-test architectures, with explicit separation of specimen temperature from cryocooler cold-head capability. Consumable use and throughput are included only where the cited sources report them.*

## Cooling arrangements and mechanical measurements

**Immersion cryostats.** A servo-hydraulic or electrodynamic frame applies force through long, aligned pull rods and grips inside a vacuum-insulated dewar. For 77 K tests, specimens and grips are submerged in LN₂; for 4 K tests, systems commonly pre-cool with LN₂, remove it and fill with LHe. ISO 6892-4 and ASTM E1450 describe immersed-helium tensile practice: keep the specimen submerged, use displacement control and limit the nominal strain rate to approximately 10⁻³ s⁻¹ or below. Immersion supplies strong thermal coupling, particularly useful during plastic deformation and prolonged fatigue, but demands cryogen transfers, level monitoring and oxygen-deficiency precautions. NIST’s published protocol used a minimum five-minute immersion soak and independently calibrated its clip gages in each liquid. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000035)

**Controlled gas and flow-through chambers.** For a selected temperature between bath boiling points, gas can be cooled by passing liquid cryogen through a heat exchanger or by expanding/vaporizing it into an insulated specimen enclosure; a sensor near the specimen, flow control and a heater establish the setpoint. This is *not equivalent* to immersing the specimen. At NASA Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC), liquid helium entered distributed, orificed tubes in an insulated fatigue-crack-growth chamber and had vaporized before leaving them: the specimen experienced **cold gaseous He at −423 °F, approximately 20 K**, not an LHe bath at 4 K. Thermocouples on both specimen faces and in the chamber monitored a reported +5/−10 °F temperature band. The rig required continuous operator monitoring and a 5,000-US-gallon helium tanker for the extended tests; that tanker capacity is **not** the amount consumed per test. KIT describes a distinct, two-chamber LN₂/LHe transfer-cooled arrangement in which the specimen is *not immersed*, specifically avoiding liquid-bubble interference with extensometer signals. (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000035)

**Liquid hydrogen.** MSFC’s Hydrogen Test Facility used a dedicated cryostat with automatic LH₂ filling to keep Inconel 718 crack-growth specimens completely submerged at −423 °F. Tests at 20 Hz followed ASTM E647; front-face clip-gage compliance tracked crack length, checked against optical measurements after testing. Direct LH₂ testing tests both **temperature and hydrogen exposure**, whereas helium gas at the same temperature is an inert thermal surrogate. In that particular alloy/test series, LH₂ and cold-He crack-growth results broadly agreed, but LH₂ testing was expensive enough that an additional desired near-threshold test was not undertaken. The source is Wells, Wright and Hastings, *NASA/TM-2005-213948* (2005); **no DOI was identified**. Precharging a specimen with hydrogen and subsequently testing it in inert helium at 20 or 4 K is likewise not testing *in* liquid hydrogen. (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000042)

**Cryogen-free, conduction-cooled rigs.** A vacuum jacket and multilayer-insulated radiation shield intercept room-temperature heat; the first cryocooler stage cools the shield, while a copper bridge or strap connects the colder stage to a specimen vessel or grips. Some designs add a small sealed charge of high-purity **helium exchange gas** to couple the specimen thermally: *no liquid helium* does not mean *no helium gas*. Thermometers must characterize the loaded specimen or its immediate fixture, since load-train conduction, contact resistance and deformation heating can leave it considerably warmer than the second-stage cold head. A Chinese two-GM system achieved a **16.8 K specimen** after about eight hours, with up to 0.3 K spatial variation, and tested Ti–6Al–4V at 20 K through quartz windows using digital image correlation (DIC). A Korean ULVAC UHE15 GM system, whose second stage is *rated* at 1.5 W at 4.2 K, took about 13 hours to reach a **20 K specimen** and reported approximately ±0.3 K control around it. The Korean studies performed metal tension and ASTM E1820 compact-specimen, unloading-compliance J-integral fracture testing, rather than demonstrating 4 K specimen tests. DOIs: [10.1088/1757-899X/278/1/012083](https://doi.org/10.1088/1757-899X/278/1/012083), [10.3390/pr10112401](https://doi.org/10.3390/pr10112401), [10.3390/met13101774](https://doi.org/10.3390/met13101774). (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000041)

**Pulse tubes:** Washington State University’s HYPER laboratory couples a **Cryomech PT-415** to an MTS Acumen 12 inside a vacuum-insulated rig, using a copper thermal strap and hydrogen liquefaction for about 20 K testing; its reported demonstrations concern **polymer composites**, although its authors say appropriately small specimens of some metals could fit. It reports up to 100 Hz fatigue capability, not a demonstrated 100 Hz metal test at 4 K. A separate Toulouse/Laboratoire National des Champs Magnétiques Intenses (LNCMI) pulse-tube installation uses a copper vessel and He exchange gas, reaches 20 K in about three hours and warms in about 4.5 hours; the reported tests are also **composites**. Its stated ability to cool to 4 K should not be cited as a demonstrated *4 K metal-test temperature*. DOI for CRAFT: [10.1088/1757-899X/1240/1/012080](https://doi.org/10.1088/1757-899X/1240/1/012080); no DOI was identified for the LNCMI abstract. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000039)

## Where the documented capabilities are

- **NIST, United States:** an MTS 55-kip (about 222 kN) servo-hydraulic frame, 100 kN load cell and three Shepic clip gages measured welded-316L tension at **77 K in LN₂ and 4 K in LHe**; the same report situates these measurements within an ASME–NASA–NIST fracture-toughness programme. It specifies three tensile specimens per weld at 77 K and two per weld at 4 K—not an annual throughput figure. DOI: [10.6028/NIST.TN.2229](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.TN.2229). (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032)
- **National High Magnetic Field Laboratory, Tallahassee:** LHe-immersed, typically **100 kN servo-hydraulic** systems perform **4 K tension, compact-tension fatigue-crack growth and J-integral fracture toughness** of magnet steels; the methods invoke ASTM E1450, E647 and E1820. DOI: [10.1088/1757-899X/279/1/012001](https://doi.org/10.1088/1757-899X/279/1/012001). (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000023)
- **NIMS and its predecessor National Research Institute for Metals, Tsukuba:** published titanium-alloy high-cycle fatigue tests used **LN₂ at 77 K and a recondensing LHe bath at 4 K**, with a ±100 kN dynamic-capacity servo-hydraulic machine; frequencies were reduced to limit specimen heating. The predecessor’s closed-loop helium-recondensing fatigue plant demonstrated **more than 460 hours** of continuous operation. DOIs: [10.1016/j.cryogenics.2005.10.011](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cryogenics.2005.10.011), [10.2355/isijinternational1966.26.48](https://doi.org/10.2355/isijinternational1966.26.48). (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030)
- **CERN Mechanical and Materials Engineering, Geneva:** four earlier **18 kN** sub-size cryostats were supplemented by an in-house **100 kN, 300–4 K** immersion cryostat for standard-size metallic tensile specimens. The 2015 account demonstrates 4 K results but presents low-temperature fracture work as an intended future use of the adaptable frame, **not** as a fracture programme demonstrated in that paper. DOI: [10.1088/1757-899X/102/1/012007](https://doi.org/10.1088/1757-899X/102/1/012007). (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000040)
- **KIT CryoMaK, Karlsruhe:** published facility ranges are **MTS 25, room temperature–7 K; MTS 50, room temperature–77 K; MTS 100, ATLAS and PHOENIX, room temperature–4.2 K**; listed facilities support combinations of tension, fatigue, fracture toughness and component testing. Its MTS 100 Landmark is rated **100 kN, up to 40 Hz**. The report described integration of that particular new cryostat as planned for 2016, so the table of facility capabilities should not be read as proof that *every* newly listed configuration was commissioned in 2015. DOI: [10.12776/ams.v21i4.650](https://doi.org/10.12776/ams.v21i4.650). (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000018)
- **NASA MSFC, Alabama:** the Hydrogen Test Facility demonstrated direct **20 K LH₂** metal crack-growth tests; a separate continuous-flow cold-He chamber produced **20 K** inert comparison tests. **NASA Glenn, Ohio:** its later cryogen-free **LESTR** uses an Instron ElectroPuls E10000 and a Sumitomo closed-cycle cooler for **40–125 K metal-wire** tension and bend/fatigue work—not 20 K or 4 K. DOI for LESTR: [10.64631/lhoi2310](https://doi.org/10.64631/lhoi2310); MSFC report: *NASA/TM-2005-213948*, no DOI identified. (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000045, pqac-00000048)
- **UK National Physical Laboratory:** its published **250 kN, ambient-to-4 K** static/dynamic mechanical cryostat is a **capability design/requirements study**, including controlled intermediate temperatures, not evidence in that report of commissioned metal tests. DOI: [10.47120/npl.mat102](https://doi.org/10.47120/npl.mat102). (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007)

## Strain, crack-opening and temperature instrumentation

Direct cryogenic strain measurement is preferred to inferring specimen strain from actuator travel, which includes load-train compliance and thermal contraction. Reported implementations include NIST’s **three Shepic ball-ended clip gages** on 25.4 mm-gage rings, calibrated separately at 77 and 4 K; NHMFL’s **Shepic clip-on extensometers** for tension and clip-on crack-opening-displacement (COD) gages for compact specimens; CERN’s **CEME C-shaped 50 mm and W-shaped 25 mm extensometers**, calibrated at room temperature, 77 and 4 K; and **Epsilon Model 3442, 10 mm** gages in the Korean 20 K studies. KIT describes in-house clip-on instruments with **350 Ω strain-gage Wheatstone bridges** and temperature-dependent calibration. Fracture tests additionally require measured load-line displacement/COD and validated crack-length tracking, particularly where discontinuous yielding upsets unloading compliance. (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000040)

Bonded cryogenic strain gages need temperature-dependent gage-factor and thermal-output correction; opposed gages can help diagnose bending, and the load train must be checked for axial alignment. Optical DIC avoids mounting a contact extensometer on the specimen but requires insulated windows and a stable speckle image; the Chinese study explicitly compared 20 K DIC with two Epsilon extensometers. A cold-stage reading alone is insufficient during serrated yielding or cyclic heating: NIMS measured internal specimen temperature rise with an embedded thermocouple, and the Korean investigators deliberately slowed tension to **5 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹** in their 304L study. (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000040)

**Commercial equipment actually named in methods** includes MTS and Instron frames; **Walter + bai** 100 kN-static/80 kN-dynamic frames; **SUNS PLS 100**; **ULVAC UHE15** GM, **Cryomech PT-415** pulse-tube and **Sumitomo CH-110LT** cryocoolers; **Epsilon**, **Shepic** and CEME-developed extensometers; and **Lake Shore Model 335** temperature control. CERN’s 100 kN cryostat and KIT’s described cryogenic hardware are institutionally built/integrated; the cited studies do not establish a commercial maker for those cryostats. KIT also lists Galdabini and INSTRON CEAST impact machines, but those should **not** be mislabelled as its 4 K fatigue frames. (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000048)

Its optimized initial closure took about **six hours**, exchange/reclosure about **two hours**, and continuous operation exceeded **460 hours**. These figures describe different accounting boundaries and must not be compared as though all were LHe *per specimen*. (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000034)

NPL’s **25–30 L LHe during an optimized 30-minute cooldown** is a *design estimate* for a proposed roughly 20–25 L dewar, not a measured cost or consumption per completed test. GM-cooled metal rigs avoid LHe purchases but reported **8–13-hour cooldowns** and still use small amounts of exchange He gas, electricity and cryocooler infrastructure. LH₂ requires dedicated storage, venting, detection and safety systems; MSFC explicitly notes the expense of additional LH₂ tests. The retrieved primary studies provide **no comparable currency-denominated capital price, helium price per litre, or fully burdened cost per metal specimen**; deriving one without local supply, recovery, labour and duty-cycle data would be misleading. ISO 6892-3:2015 covers tensile testing from +10 °C to −196 °C and specifies cooling by refrigeration, compressed-gas expansion such as CO2 or N2, or immersion in a boiling-point liquid such as nitrogen. Specimens should be cooled to the specified temperature and soaked for 10 minutes. Temperature instrumentation should be calibrated and verified annually, with resolution of 1 °C or better; accuracy requirements are ±2 °C from +10 °C to −40 °C and ±3 °C from −41 °C to −196 °C. ISO 6892-4:2015 covers tensile testing in liquid helium at −269 °C (4 K), using a mechanical cryostat, special instrumentation, and sub-size specimens. Samples are fully immersed in LHe and tested in displacement control at a nominal strain rate of 10−3 s−1 or less. The cryostat is pre-cooled with LN2 to its boiling point (−196 °C, 77 K), after which nitrogen is removed and LHe is transferred until specimens and grips are immersed. Specimens remain at 4 K throughout testing. Alignment is emphasized, with maximum acceptable bending strain designated Class 10 under ISO 23788. contexts.context: This excerpt documents a CERN cryostat designed primarily for low-temperature uniaxial tensile testing, rather than fracture-toughness or fatigue testing. The load train uses shoulder-headed sample holders and ball joints to maintain specimen alignment and reduce bending moments. The pulling rod is grade 5 titanium, with Ra < 1.6 μm surface roughness to limit friction at the rubber O-ring seal. Extensometers are available in C- and W-shaped configurations; the C-shaped device has a 50 mm gauge length and up to 50% elongation, while both types were calibrated at 4 K, 77 K, and room temperature. Instrumentation includes four connector sets, provisions for extensometers, LVDTs, temperature sensors, strain gauges, capacitive sensors, and optical-fibre sensors. An internal Ti5Al2.5Sn ELI load cell uses a four-active-arm Wheatstone bridge with HBM 350 Ω strain-gauge rosettes. It was calibrated under ISO 376:2011 using ten loading steps up to 80 kN, repeated for six cycles, and achieved class 1 force-proving performance for ISO 6892. contexts.context: This excerpt provides primary design requirements for a cryostat-based FRP mechanical-testing apparatus at 77 K, 20 K, and 4 K. The system should operate from ambient temperature to 4 K with ±2 K control accuracy, using liquid nitrogen for temperatures down to 77 K and liquid helium below 77 K to 4 K. contexts.context: This excerpt provides primary methods details for 304L stainless-steel tensile and fracture testing in a cryogenic apparatus. The facility used a fatigue-testing machine with a cryostat capable of reaching and maintaining 20 K. Gaseous helium was introduced into the cryostat and cooled by a Gifford–McMahon cryocooler, specifically an ULVAC UHE15; the authors note that mechanical cooling uses very little gaseous helium and is relatively inexpensive. The cryostat itself had a vacuum structure made from 304L stainless steel. Testing used Walter + bai servo-hydraulic load frames rated for 100 kN static and 80 kN dynamic loading. Temperature was monitored using a silicon diode connected to a Lakeshore Model 335. Tensile tests were displacement controlled at 0.03 mm/min, corresponding to an initial strain rate of 5.0 × 10−5 s−1, to limit deformation-induced heating. Deformation was measured with an Epsilon Model 3442 extensometer having a 10 mm gauge length. Tests began 30 minutes after reaching the prescribed temperature, with target temperatures of 20, 77, and 300 K. Fracture toughness was measured by the unloading-compliance method on a single compact specimen, using ASTM E1820-21 J-integral procedures. Compact specimens were fatigue-precracked at 5 Hz to a0/W = 0.6, with a minimum stress-intensity factor of 33 MPa m1/2. The excerpt does not provide 4 K results, pulse-tube cooling, LN2/LHe immersion, liquid-hydrogen testing, gas-flow chambers, named external facilities, throughput, or helium-consumption figures. contexts.context: This excerpt provides primary-method information for CERN’s cryogenic uniaxial tensile-testing apparatus, but it does not describe fracture-toughness or fatigue testing, 20 K operation, liquid-nitrogen/liquid-helium immersion, cryocoolers, gas-flow chambers, liquid-hydrogen tests, or comparisons among NASA, NIMS, KIT, the National High Magnetic Field Laboratory, and NIST. The apparatus is a 100 kN cryostat designed for 300–4 K testing and optimized for CERN’s existing UTS machine; it can also fit a standard servo-hydraulic machine. Two extensometers are described: a C-shape for standard flat specimens with a 50 mm gage length and up to 50% elongation, and a W-shape for small standard specimens with a 25 mm gage length. Both were calibrated by the supplier and in-house at 4 K, 77 K, and room temperature. Validation followed ASTM E1450 and ASTM E1012, requiring bending strain below 10% of axial strain. Testing used flat and buttonhead specimens, strain gauges, and an internal load cell. At 4 K, OFE copper had Rp0.2 = 427 MPa, UTS = 525 MPa, and elongation = 43.4%; INERMET®180 fractured elastically, with UTS = 1048 MPa and elongation = 0.4%. The article DOI is 10.1088/1757-899X/102/1/012007.

contexts.context: CryoMaK demonstrated cryogenic mechanical testing from room temperature to 4.2 K, including tensile, fatigue, fracture-toughness, impact, hardness, component and nonstandard tests. contexts.context: A 2017 study reports a “liquid helium free” cryogenic mechanical-testing system with optical windows, cryocoolers, vacuum vessel (10⁻³ Pa), helium-gas-filled sample chamber, and continuous tunability from room temperature to ~20 K. Cooling to 16.8 K required ~8 h; spatial temperature variation was ~0.3 K. Ti6Al4V tension used a servo-hydraulic load machine at 0.2 mm/min. Strain was measured by optical DIC (2592×1944-pixel camera, 41×41 subsets) and cryogenic Epsilon extensometers. At 20 K, DIC gave 139 GPa/0.33 versus extensometers’ 110 GPa/0.30. DOI: **10.1088/1757-899X/278/1/012083**.

contexts.context: Zhang et al. describe a liquid-helium-free cryogenic mechanical-testing system using two Gifford–McMahon cryocoolers, helium-gas convection, heaters/controllers, inner/outer vacuum chambers, and quartz optical windows. Temperature is continuously tunable from room temperature to approximately 20 K; Ti6Al4V tension, elastic modulus, Poisson’s ratio, and strain were measured at 20 K. Optical windows enable two-dimensional digital image correlation (DIC), avoiding opaque liquid cryostats and coolant optical distortion. DIC displacement/strain agreed with cryogenic-grade extensometers. Components include cryogenic chambers, mechanical frame, testing machine, illumination, and camera. DOI: “10.1088/1757-899X/278/1/012083.”

contexts.context: Adams et al. describe CRAFT, a Washington State University HYPER Laboratory facility for cryogenic tension and fatigue testing. It combines an **MTS-Acumen 12 electrodynamic 12-kN load frame** with a vacuum chamber, stainless-steel bellows, G10 insulation, thermal straps, indium seals, and grips. CRAFT liquefies hydrogen, reaches approximately **14 K** (near hydrogen’s triple point), and performs tension–tension/tension–compression fatigue to **100 Hz**; static and dynamic forces are **8.5 and 12 kN**, respectively. The chamber is **2.25 in diameter × 9 in high**, with **10⁻⁵ Pa** vacuum. Citation: Adams, Hunt & Leachman (2022), DOI **10.1088/1757-899X/1240/1/012080**.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides primary evidence for KIT’s CryoMaK facility, but no evidence for CERN, NIMS, NASA MSFC, the National High Magnetic Field Laboratory, NIST, or other US national laboratories. CryoMaK supports cryogenic testing from room temperature down to 4.2 K, including quasi-static and dynamic mechanical tests: tensile, fatigue, fracture toughness, instrumented impact, hardness, component, and non-standard tests. The described low-temperature measurement uses specimens fitted with extensometers in a liquid-helium-bath cryostat. Testing is conducted while the cryostat slowly warms as liquid helium evaporates, with the authors stating that the system remains in thermal equilibrium throughout a 12-hour warm-up to 290 K. The extensometers use 350-ohm strain gauges; they are calibrated before each measurement series, with temperature-dependent calibration factors fitted by a polynomial. Length changes are converted to specimen deformation in millimeters using those factors. The excerpt identifies MTS 100, Galdabini 450, INSTRON CEAST 9350, and INNOVATEST NEXUS 4302 as CryoMaK equipment added in 2014. It does not state helium consumption, operating cost, test throughput, gas-flow chamber performance, or specimen temperature validation for 4 K cryocooler-driven metal rigs. contexts.context: The excerpt documents cryogenic tensile testing of 316L welds, not fracture toughness or fatigue. contexts.context: At NHMFL, all 4 K tensile and fracture-toughness tests use servo-hydraulic machines with a load-reaction frame and liquid-helium cryostat. A typical 100 kN load cell serves tensile and load-line compact-tension specimens for fatigue-crack-growth-rate (FCGR) and fracture tests. Shepic clip-on extensometers measure tensile strain; clip-on crack-opening-displacement gauges measure CT load-line displacement. Procedures follow ASTM E1450 (tension), E647 (FCGR), and E1820 (fracture toughness); commercial software calculates \(K_{IC(J)}\) by the J-integral method. Citation: IOP Conf. Ser. contexts.context: The 1986 ISIJ facility used a hydraulic servo-pulse, load-controlled fatigue machine (dynamic ±5 t, static ±7.5 t, 0.01–50 Hz) with a vacuum-insulated cryostat shielded by forced-flow liquid nitrogen. A three-stage Claude/Joule–Thomson helium refrigerator supplied 20 W at 4.4 K without external coolant or thermal shield; purified helium used molecular-sieve and LN₂-cooled charcoal adsorbers. Specimens were held in a dual-cylinder grip (>100 Hz natural frequency) to prevent vibration. Cooldown initially required 17 h; optimized operation reached cryostat closure in 6 h, with specimen exchange requiring about 2 h. No DOI is provided in the excerpt.

contexts.context: A 1986 Kobe Steel fatigue facility used a closed cryostat/refrigerator with liquid-nitrogen shielding and liquid-helium cooling/recondensation. Initial consumption was approximately 300 kg LN₂ and 50 L LHe; afterward, shielding required ~15 kg LN₂/h, with no additional helium supply. Specimen exchange required warming, helium addition (~15 L), and LN₂ precooling. A HITACHI MB-6890 processor, YHP3497A data-acquisition unit, platinum-resistance thermometers, and chromel-alumel thermocouples monitored 17 temperatures, helium level, JT-valve opening, and gas flow. Tests ran at 4 Hz; fatigue rupture exceeded one week (2×10⁶ cycles) and 460 h continuous operation. No DOI is supplied.

contexts.context: Ogata and Ishikawa describe an NIRIM Tsukuba liquid-helium fatigue machine (1983; published *Transactions ISIJ* 26, 1986), using a compressor, purifier, 1-m³ gas holder, refrigerator, and cryostat with an internal recondenser. A JT valve produces helium mist; evaporated gas is re-liquefied in a closed loop, maintaining constant level without additions and enabling over 460 h continuous operation. The compressor reaches ~1.7 MPa and 300 Nm³/h; refrigerator stages provide ~60, 30, and 8 K before JT expansion. Conventional replenished-liquid-helium testing is simpler but consumes large quantities. No DOI is provided.

contexts.context: At Stuttgart University, tensile tests on 304LN/316LN were conducted in liquid hydrogen and gaseous helium at 20 K; liquid hydrogen reduced elongation by 2–4% and area reductions were 61% (304LN) and 77% (316LN) relative to gaseous helium [18]. The study developed a vacuum-jacketed tensile cryostat using helium gas to simulate a 20-K liquid-hydrogen environment and tested hydrogen-charged stainless steels/aluminum. ASTM E8/E8M subsize specimens used 10-mm gauge lengths and an Epsilon 3442 axial extensometer (Epsilon Technology Corp.). No DOI or commercial load-frame/cryocooler details appear in this excerpt.

contexts.context: The 2023 *Metals* study used a 304L stainless-steel fatigue/fracture setup with a vacuum 304L cryostat, gaseous helium, and an ULVAC UHE15 Gifford–McMahon cryocooler, reaching 20 K with little helium consumption. Walter + bai servo-hydraulic frames provided 100 kN static/80 kN dynamic capacity. Temperatures were 20, 77, and 300 K; tests began 30 minutes after stabilization. Temperature was monitored using a silicon diode and Lake Shore Model 335. Tensile strain used an Epsilon Model 3442 extensometer (10-mm gauge); crosshead speed was 0.03 mm/min (5×10⁻⁵ s⁻¹). Fracture testing followed ASTM E1820-21 unloading compliance. Citation: *Metals* 13 (2023) 1774; DOI not shown in excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies liquid nitrogen (77 K), liquid hydrogen (20 K), and liquid helium (4 K) as cryogens; heaters can raise temperatures. Because hydrogen is flammable/explosive, helium gas is preferred above 20 K. Mechanical cooling uses a Gifford–McMahon cryocooler: the cited rig reached 20 K in 10 h with little gaseous helium and was considered low-cost. Its evacuated cryostat (10⁻⁵ Torr) used copper/304 stainless vessels, aluminum radiation shielding with 30-layer insulation, and a ULVAC UHE15 (45 W at 50 K; 1.5 W at 4.2 K). Walter+bai servo-hydraulic frames provided 100 kN static/80 kN dynamic capacity; Lakeshore 335 controlled silicon-diode temperature. References [38–39] are cited, but no DOI appears.

ASTM E1450 [18] covers cryogen safety. Vacuum-insulated dewars/transfer lines are required; helium may be vented, recycled, or reliquefied. Cooling method affects results and throughput. No commercial makers, facilities, costs, liquid-hydrogen testing, cryocoolers, or DOIs are specified.

contexts.context: The study tested A286 and Alloy 718 by slow-strain-rate tension at room temperature and 4.2 K (3×10⁻⁵ s⁻¹), using a liquid-helium cryostat surrounded by a liquid-nitrogen-cooled radiation shield for constant specimen temperature. Strain-to-failure at 4.2 K came from crosshead displacement (±1.25% strain) because a clip-on extensometer slipped; interpolated strains were required. Hydrogen charging used an autoclave at 1000 bar, 473 K for 14 days. No manufacturers, costs, throughput, 20/77 K, fatigue/fracture-toughness facilities, or DOI are provided.

contexts.context: CERN’s 100-kN cryostat enables uniaxial tensile testing from 300 K to 4 K in a standard servo-hydraulic/load-frame machine, using in-house tooling for flat and round specimens. C- and W-shaped CEME extensometers accommodate 50-mm/50%-elongation and 25-mm gage lengths, respectively, and were calibrated at 4 K, 77 K, and room temperature. Strain measurement used glued strain gauges in half-bridge circuits; buttonheads used eight gauges, paired at cryogenic temperature. ASTM E1450/E1012 validation kept bending below 10%. Capacity is ≥800 lbf (3,559 N), for 0.050–0.085-in wires; Unit 01 supports <50 tensile cycles or 100,000 bend cycles without maintenance. contexts.context: This excerpt documents CERN’s Santillana et al. 2015 cryogenic tensile-testing system, but it does not provide an exact liquid-helium consumption per test, cooldown time, reconfiguration or testing throughput, monetary costs, or commercial names for the load frame, cryocooler, or cryostat. It identifies the apparatus as a custom 100 kN cryostat designed for uniaxial testing from 300 K down to 4 K, intended to fit CERN’s existing UTS machine and a standard servo-hydraulic machine. The extensometers are CEME-developed C-shape and W-shape designs, calibrated at 4 K, 77 K, and room temperature. The C-shape serves 50 mm-gage standard flat specimens, while the W-shape serves 25 mm-gage small specimens. Validation at room temperature showed bending generally below the ASTM E1450 limit of 10% of axial strain. At 4 K, OFE copper showed Rp0.2 = 427 MPa, UTS = 525 MPa, and elongation A = 43.4%, with discontinuous plastic flow. INERMET®180 fractured in the elastic region, preventing yield-strength calculation, and had UTS = 1048 MPa and A = 0.4%. Thus, this excerpt supports a contrast between brittle tungsten-alloy behavior and highly ductile OFE-copper behavior at 4 K, but contains no direct 20 K comparison or cryogen-free performance data.

(2015) excerpt documents the design and instrumentation of CERN’s cryogenic tensile-testing cryostat, but it does not provide an exact liquid-helium quantity consumed per test, cooldown duration, reconfiguration throughput, or actual monetary costs. It also does not identify commercial brands or models for the load frame, cryocooler, or cryostat. Relevant commercial component information includes 3M connectors, Fischer instrumentation feedthrough connections, and HBM 1-XC11-3/350 strain-gage rosettes used in the internal load cell. The extensometers are identified by form factor rather than a commercial model: C-shape and W-shape devices developed by CERN’s Cryogenic Engineering & Materials Expertise (CEME). The C-shape version has a 50 mm gauge length and the W-shape version a 25 mm gauge length; both were calibrated at 4 K, 77 K, and room temperature. The excerpt describes grade 5 titanium for the pulling rod and Ti5Al2.5Sn ELI for the internal load cell, emphasizing low-temperature strength, ductility, toughness, and reduced heat conduction. It reports calibration of the internal load cell through ten loading steps up to 80 kN, repeated for six cycles, achieving class 1 performance. No comparative mechanical outcomes for metal specimens tested at 4 K versus 20 K, nor cryogen-free versus liquid-helium operation, are presented in this excerpt.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: What equipment and facilities are used for cryogenic mechanical testing of metals (tension, fracture toughness, fatigue) at 77 K, 20 K and 4 K? Cover liquid-nitrogen and liquid-helium immersion cryostats, cold-gas flow-through environmental chambers, cryocooler (Gifford-McMahon or pulse-tube) conduction-cooled rigs that need no liquid helium, and testing in liquid hydrogen; strain measurement and extensometry at cryogenic temperature; the commercial makers named in methods sections (load frames, cryostats, cryocoolers); the main documented test facilities (national labs, NASA centers, magnet labs, CERN, KIT, NIMS) with their temperature ranges; and cost, helium use and throughput where reported. Give citations and DOIs.

# Cryogenic mechanical testing of metals: equipment and facilities

**The operating distinction is the specimen environment, not merely the refrigerator rating.** Liquid-nitrogen immersion provides approximately 77 K; liquid-helium immersion provides approximately 4.2 K. Tests near 20 K can instead use temperature-controlled helium gas or direct liquid-hydrogen immersion. A Gifford–McMahon (GM) or pulse-tube cold head rated near 4 K does **not** establish that a loaded metal specimen reaches or remains at 4 K. The cited cryogen-free metal tests demonstrate approximately 20 K; the documented 4 K bulk-metal tension, fatigue and fracture tests principally use liquid helium. (perez2022mechanicaltestingof pages 12-15, zhang2017liquidheliumfree pages 1-3, narbonneUnknownyearnovelmethodfor pages 1-2, mcrae2017fatigueandfracture pages 3-4, kim2022metallicmaterialevaluation pages 4-5)

The following comparison separates measured operation from proposed capability. Its cited studies and DOIs are discussed below. (perez2022mechanicaltestingof pages 18-21, sas2015cryomak–theoverviewof pages 1-3, mcrae2017fatigueandfracture pages 3-4, wells2005fatiguecrackgrowth pages 6-9, weeks2022tensiletestsat pages 8-12, santillana2015designandfabrication pages 4-6, kim2023tensileandfracture pages 4-6, adams2022cryogenicacceleratedfatigue pages 4-7)

| Cooling architecture | Demonstrated specimen temperature | Metal mechanical application and named equipment/facility | Cryogen / throughput actually reported | Primary study DOI |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| LN₂/LHe bath immersion | 77 K / 4 K | **NIST:** welded 316L tensile tests; MTS 55-kip servo-hydraulic frame, 100-kN load cell, three Shepic clip gages. **NHMFL:** tensile, fatigue-crack growth and fracture toughness; 100-kN servo-hydraulic systems, Shepic extensometers/COD gage. (mcrae2017fatigueandfracture pages 3-4, weeks2022tensiletestsat pages 8-12) | NIST specimens soaked fully immersed for ≥5 min; no consumption or throughput reported. NHMFL consumption not reported. | [10.6028/NIST.TN.2229](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.TN.2229); [10.1088/1757-899X/279/1/012001](https://doi.org/10.1088/1757-899X/279/1/012001) |
| Recondensing LHe bath with LN₂ shield | 4 K | **NIMS predecessor, NRIM Tsukuba:** high-cycle metal fatigue; hydraulic servo-pulse machine, ±5-t dynamic load, 0.01–50 Hz, closed-loop helium refrigerator/recondenser. (ogata1986anewliquid pages 1-2, ogata1986anewliquid pages 2-4) | Startup: ≈50 L LHe and ≈300 kg LN₂; shield ≈15 kg LN₂/h; ≈15 L LHe added after specimen exchange; no LHe addition during uninterrupted testing; specimen exchange ≈2 h; >460 h continuous operation. (ogata1986anewliquid pages 4-5) | [10.2355/isijinternational1966.26.48](https://doi.org/10.2355/isijinternational1966.26.48) |
| LN₂/LHe immersion cryostat | 77 K / 4 K | **CERN MME:** standardized metal tension in an in-house 100-kN cryostat; CEME C- and W-shaped extensometers calibrated at RT, 77 K and 4 K. (santillana2015designandfabrication pages 1-4, santillana2015designandfabrication pages 9-11) | 25–30 L LHe per test; 20–25 min cooldown between tests at 1.2–1.3 bar; ≈15-L internal cryostat volume. (santillana2015designandfabrication pages 4-6) | [10.1088/1757-899X/102/1/012007](https://doi.org/10.1088/1757-899X/102/1/012007) |
| Two-stage transfer cooling: separate LN₂ and LHe chambers; specimen not immersed | RT→77 K→4.2 K | **KIT CryoMaK:** tensile, fatigue, fatigue-crack growth and fracture toughness; MTS 25/50/100, ATLAS 650-kN and PHOENIX 100-kN facilities; MTS 100 Landmark rated 100 kN and 40 Hz. (sas2015cryomak–theoverviewof pages 1-3, sas2015cryomak–theoverviewof media 78b803da) | Cryogen quantities and cost not reported. Avoiding immersion suppresses coolant bubbles that can disturb extensometer signals. (sas2015cryomak–theoverviewof pages 3-8) | [10.12776/ams.v21i4.650](https://doi.org/10.12776/ams.v21i4.650) |
| Cold-He spray/flow chamber versus direct LH₂ immersion | 20 K (−423 °F) | **NASA MSFC:** Inconel 718 fatigue-crack-growth tests on digitally controlled servo-hydraulic machines; cold-He rig used distributed orifice tubes, while the Hydrogen Test Facility automatically maintained full LH₂ submersion. (wells2005fatiguecrackgrowth pages 6-9, wells2005fatiguecrackgrowth pages 9-13) | Cold-He rig required continuous LHe from a 5,000-gal tanker and continuous monitoring; no per-test volume stated. LH₂ tests ran at 20 Hz; expense prevented another low-ΔK test. | NASA/TM-2005-213948 — **no DOI reported** |
| Cryogen-free GM cooling with static He exchange gas | 20 K metal specimen; cold head rated at 4.2 K, but **not** a demonstrated 4-K metal test | **Korea:** 304L/316L and Al-alloy tension; 304L tension and J-integral fracture; ULVAC UHE15 GM cryocooler, Walter + bai 100-kN-static/80-kN-dynamic frame, Lake Shore 335 and Epsilon 3442 extensometer. A related Chinese system used two GM coolers and a SUNS PLS 100 frame for Ti-6Al-4V tension/DIC. (zhang2017liquidheliumfree pages 1-3, zhang2017liquidheliumfree pages 3-6, kim2022metallicmaterialevaluation pages 4-5, kim2023tensileandfracture pages 4-6) | Only a small sealed charge of 99.999% He gas; quantity/cost not stated. Cooldown ≈13 h in the Korean rig and ≈8 h to 16.8 K in the Chinese rig; Korean test-zone control ±0.3 K. (zhang2017liquidheliumfree pages 6-9, kim2022metallicmaterialevaluation pages 5-9) | [10.3390/pr10112401](https://doi.org/10.3390/pr10112401); [10.1088/1757-899X/278/1/012083](https://doi.org/10.1088/1757-899X/278/1/012083) |
| Pulse-tube conduction cooling | **WSU CRAFT:** ≈14–20 K; **LNCMI:** demonstrated 20 K, although cooler can reach 4 K. **No evidenced 4-K metal specimen test in either source.** | **WSU HYPER CRAFT:** composites only, Cryomech PT-415 plus MTS Acumen 12, tension/fatigue to 100 Hz while liquefying H₂. **LNCMI/ICA:** composites only, pulse-tube cooler, He exchange gas, tension/compression/shear. (adams2022cryogenicacceleratedfatigue pages 1-4, narbonneUnknownyearnovelmethodfor pages 1-2, adams2022cryogenicacceleratedfatigue pages 4-7) | CRAFT stores feed H₂ in four cylinders totaling 196 L; per-test LH₂ use not stated. ## Cooling arrangements and mechanical measurements

**Immersion cryostats.** A servo-hydraulic or electrodynamic frame applies force through long, aligned pull rods and grips inside a vacuum-insulated dewar. For 77 K tests, specimens and grips are submerged in LN₂; for 4 K tests, systems commonly pre-cool with LN₂, remove it and fill with LHe. ISO 6892-4 and ASTM E1450 describe immersed-helium tensile practice: keep the specimen submerged, use displacement control and limit the nominal strain rate to approximately 10⁻³ s⁻¹ or below. Immersion supplies strong thermal coupling, particularly useful during plastic deformation and prolonged fatigue, but demands cryogen transfers, level monitoring and oxygen-deficiency precautions. NIST’s published protocol used a minimum five-minute immersion soak and independently calibrated its clip gages in each liquid. (perez2022mechanicaltestingof pages 12-15, perez2022mechanicaltestingof pages 15-18, weeks2022tensiletestsat pages 8-12, perez2022mechanicaltestingof pages 21-23)

**Controlled gas and flow-through chambers.** For a selected temperature between bath boiling points, gas can be cooled by passing liquid cryogen through a heat exchanger or by expanding/vaporizing it into an insulated specimen enclosure; a sensor near the specimen, flow control and a heater establish the setpoint. This is *not equivalent* to immersing the specimen. At NASA Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC), liquid helium entered distributed, orificed tubes in an insulated fatigue-crack-growth chamber and had vaporized before leaving them: the specimen experienced **cold gaseous He at −423 °F, approximately 20 K**, not an LHe bath at 4 K. Thermocouples on both specimen faces and in the chamber monitored a reported +5/−10 °F temperature band. The rig required continuous operator monitoring and a 5,000-US-gallon helium tanker for the extended tests; that tanker capacity is **not** the amount consumed per test. KIT describes a distinct, two-chamber LN₂/LHe transfer-cooled arrangement in which the specimen is *not immersed*, specifically avoiding liquid-bubble interference with extensometer signals. (sas2015cryomak–theoverviewof pages 3-8, wells2005fatiguecrackgrowth pages 6-9, perez2022mechanicaltestingof pages 21-23)

**Liquid hydrogen.** MSFC’s Hydrogen Test Facility used a dedicated cryostat with automatic LH₂ filling to keep Inconel 718 crack-growth specimens completely submerged at −423 °F. Tests at 20 Hz followed ASTM E647; front-face clip-gage compliance tracked crack length, checked against optical measurements after testing. Direct LH₂ testing tests both **temperature and hydrogen exposure**, whereas helium gas at the same temperature is an inert thermal surrogate. In that particular alloy/test series, LH₂ and cold-He crack-growth results broadly agreed, but LH₂ testing was expensive enough that an additional desired near-threshold test was not undertaken. The source is Wells, Wright and Hastings, *NASA/TM-2005-213948* (2005); **no DOI was identified**. Precharging a specimen with hydrogen and subsequently testing it in inert helium at 20 or 4 K is likewise not testing *in* liquid hydrogen. (wells2005fatiguecrackgrowth pages 6-9, wells2005fatiguecrackgrowth pages 9-13, kim2022metallicmaterialevaluation pages 2-4, damm2025hydrogen–dislocationinteractionsat pages 4-7)

**Cryogen-free, conduction-cooled rigs.** A vacuum jacket and multilayer-insulated radiation shield intercept room-temperature heat; the first cryocooler stage cools the shield, while a copper bridge or strap connects the colder stage to a specimen vessel or grips. Some designs add a small sealed charge of high-purity **helium exchange gas** to couple the specimen thermally: *no liquid helium* does not mean *no helium gas*. Thermometers must characterize the loaded specimen or its immediate fixture, since load-train conduction, contact resistance and deformation heating can leave it considerably warmer than the second-stage cold head. A Chinese two-GM system achieved a **16.8 K specimen** after about eight hours, with up to 0.3 K spatial variation, and tested Ti–6Al–4V at 20 K through quartz windows using digital image correlation (DIC). A Korean ULVAC UHE15 GM system, whose second stage is *rated* at 1.5 W at 4.2 K, took about 13 hours to reach a **20 K specimen** and reported approximately ±0.3 K control around it. The Korean studies performed metal tension and ASTM E1820 compact-specimen, unloading-compliance J-integral fracture testing, rather than demonstrating 4 K specimen tests. DOIs: [10.1088/1757-899X/278/1/012083](https://doi.org/10.1088/1757-899X/278/1/012083), [10.3390/pr10112401](https://doi.org/10.3390/pr10112401), [10.3390/met13101774](https://doi.org/10.3390/met13101774). (zhang2017liquidheliumfree pages 6-9, zhang2017liquidheliumfree pages 1-3, zhang2017liquidheliumfree pages 3-6, kim2022metallicmaterialevaluation pages 4-5, kim2023tensileandfracture pages 4-6, kim2022metallicmaterialevaluation pages 5-9)

**Pulse tubes:** Washington State University’s HYPER laboratory couples a **Cryomech PT-415** to an MTS Acumen 12 inside a vacuum-insulated rig, using a copper thermal strap and hydrogen liquefaction for about 20 K testing; its reported demonstrations concern **polymer composites**, although its authors say appropriately small specimens of some metals could fit. It reports up to 100 Hz fatigue capability, not a demonstrated 100 Hz metal test at 4 K. A separate Toulouse/Laboratoire National des Champs Magnétiques Intenses (LNCMI) pulse-tube installation uses a copper vessel and He exchange gas, reaches 20 K in about three hours and warms in about 4.5 hours; the reported tests are also **composites**. Its stated ability to cool to 4 K should not be cited as a demonstrated *4 K metal-test temperature*. DOI for CRAFT: [10.1088/1757-899X/1240/1/012080](https://doi.org/10.1088/1757-899X/1240/1/012080); no DOI was identified for the LNCMI abstract. (adams2022cryogenicacceleratedfatigue pages 1-4, narbonneUnknownyearnovelmethodfor pages 1-2, adams2022cryogenicacceleratedfatigue pages 4-7)

## Where the documented capabilities are

- **NIST, United States:** an MTS 55-kip (about 222 kN) servo-hydraulic frame, 100 kN load cell and three Shepic clip gages measured welded-316L tension at **77 K in LN₂ and 4 K in LHe**; the same report situates these measurements within an ASME–NASA–NIST fracture-toughness programme. It specifies three tensile specimens per weld at 77 K and two per weld at 4 K—not an annual throughput figure. DOI: [10.6028/NIST.TN.2229](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.TN.2229). (weeks2022tensiletestsat pages 6-8, weeks2022tensiletestsat pages 8-12)
- **National High Magnetic Field Laboratory, Tallahassee:** LHe-immersed, typically **100 kN servo-hydraulic** systems perform **4 K tension, compact-tension fatigue-crack growth and J-integral fracture toughness** of magnet steels; the methods invoke ASTM E1450, E647 and E1820. DOI: [10.1088/1757-899X/279/1/012001](https://doi.org/10.1088/1757-899X/279/1/012001). (mcrae2017fatigueandfracture pages 1-3, mcrae2017fatigueandfracture pages 3-4)
- **NIMS and its predecessor National Research Institute for Metals, Tsukuba:** published titanium-alloy high-cycle fatigue tests used **LN₂ at 77 K and a recondensing LHe bath at 4 K**, with a ±100 kN dynamic-capacity servo-hydraulic machine; frequencies were reduced to limit specimen heating. The predecessor’s closed-loop helium-recondensing fatigue plant demonstrated **more than 460 hours** of continuous operation. DOIs: [10.1016/j.cryogenics.2005.10.011](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cryogenics.2005.10.011), [10.2355/isijinternational1966.26.48](https://doi.org/10.2355/isijinternational1966.26.48). (yuri2006notcheffectson pages 1-3, ogata1986anewliquid pages 1-2, ogata1986anewliquid pages 4-5)
- **CERN Mechanical and Materials Engineering, Geneva:** four earlier **18 kN** sub-size cryostats were supplemented by an in-house **100 kN, 300–4 K** immersion cryostat for standard-size metallic tensile specimens. The 2015 account demonstrates 4 K results but presents low-temperature fracture work as an intended future use of the adaptable frame, **not** as a fracture programme demonstrated in that paper. DOI: [10.1088/1757-899X/102/1/012007](https://doi.org/10.1088/1757-899X/102/1/012007). (santillana2015designandfabrication pages 1-4, santillana2015designandfabrication pages 9-11)

Its MTS 100 Landmark is rated **100 kN, up to 40 Hz**. The report described integration of that particular new cryostat as planned for 2016, so the table of facility capabilities should not be read as proof that *every* newly listed configuration was commissioned in 2015. ## Strain, crack-opening and temperature instrumentation

Direct cryogenic strain measurement is preferred to inferring specimen strain from actuator travel, which includes load-train compliance and thermal contraction. Reported implementations include NIST’s **three Shepic ball-ended clip gages** on 25.4 mm-gage rings, calibrated separately at 77 and 4 K; NHMFL’s **Shepic clip-on extensometers** for tension and clip-on crack-opening-displacement (COD) gages for compact specimens; CERN’s **CEME C-shaped 50 mm and W-shaped 25 mm extensometers**, calibrated at room temperature, 77 and 4 K; and **Epsilon Model 3442, 10 mm** gages in the Korean 20 K studies. KIT describes in-house clip-on instruments with **350 Ω strain-gage Wheatstone bridges** and temperature-dependent calibration. Fracture tests additionally require measured load-line displacement/COD and validated crack-length tracking, particularly where discontinuous yielding upsets unloading compliance. (sas2015cryomak–theoverviewof pages 3-8, sas2015cryomak–theoverviewof pages 8-9, mcrae2017fatigueandfracture pages 3-4, weeks2022tensiletestsat pages 8-12, kim2022metallicmaterialevaluation pages 2-4, kim2023tensileandfracture pages 4-6, santillana2015designandfabrication pages 9-11)

Bonded cryogenic strain gages need temperature-dependent gage-factor and thermal-output correction; opposed gages can help diagnose bending, and the load train must be checked for axial alignment. Optical DIC avoids mounting a contact extensometer on the specimen but requires insulated windows and a stable speckle image; the Chinese study explicitly compared 20 K DIC with two Epsilon extensometers. A cold-stage reading alone is insufficient during serrated yielding or cyclic heating: NIMS measured internal specimen temperature rise with an embedded thermocouple, and the Korean investigators deliberately slowed tension to **5 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹** in their 304L study. (zhang2017liquidheliumfree pages 6-9, zhang2017liquidheliumfree pages 3-6, ogata1986anewliquid pages 4-5, perez2022mechanicaltestingof pages 21-23, kim2023tensileandfracture pages 4-6, santillana2015designandfabrication pages 9-11)

**Commercial equipment actually named in methods** includes MTS and Instron frames; **Walter + bai** 100 kN-static/80 kN-dynamic frames; **SUNS PLS 100**; **ULVAC UHE15** GM, **Cryomech PT-415** pulse-tube and **Sumitomo CH-110LT** cryocoolers; **Epsilon**, **Shepic** and CEME-developed extensometers; and **Lake Shore Model 335** temperature control. CERN’s 100 kN cryostat and KIT’s described cryogenic hardware are institutionally built/integrated; the cited studies do not establish a commercial maker for those cryostats. KIT also lists Galdabini and INSTRON CEAST impact machines, but those should **not** be mislabelled as its 4 K fatigue frames. (zhang2017liquidheliumfree pages 3-6, sas2015cryomak–theoverviewof pages 1-3, mcrae2017fatigueandfracture pages 3-4, weeks2022tensiletestsat pages 8-12, santillana2015designandfabrication pages 1-4, kim2022metallicmaterialevaluation pages 4-5, kim2023tensileandfracture pages 4-6, adams2022cryogenicacceleratedfatigue pages 4-7, ring2026mechanicaldesignand pages 26-28)

## Helium, time and cost: what is actually reported

CERN calculated **25–30 L of LHe for one test** in its approximately **15 L** cryostat, with **20–25 minutes of cooldown between tests** at the specified filling pressure; this is a turnaround component, not the duration of every test. The NIMS predecessor reported about **50 L LHe and 300 kg LN₂ at startup**, approximately **15 kg LN₂ per hour** for shielding, and roughly **15 L LHe added after exchanging a specimen**, while requiring **no added LHe during uninterrupted recondensing operation**. Its optimized initial closure took about **six hours**, exchange/reclosure about **two hours**, and continuous operation exceeded **460 hours**. These figures describe different accounting boundaries and must not be compared as though all were LHe *per specimen*. (ogata1986anewliquid pages 1-2, ogata1986anewliquid pages 2-4, ogata1986anewliquid pages 4-5, santillana2015designandfabrication pages 4-6)

NPL’s **25–30 L LHe during an optimized 30-minute cooldown** is a *design estimate* for a proposed roughly 20–25 L dewar, not a measured cost or consumption per completed test. GM-cooled metal rigs avoid LHe purchases but reported **8–13-hour cooldowns** and still use small amounts of exchange He gas, electricity and cryocooler infrastructure. LH₂ requires dedicated storage, venting, detection and safety systems; MSFC explicitly notes the expense of additional LH₂ tests. The retrieved primary studies provide **no comparable currency-denominated capital price, helium price per litre, or fully burdened cost per metal specimen**; deriving one without local supply, recovery, labour and duty-cycle data would be misleading. (perez2022mechanicaltestingof pages 18-21, zhang2017liquidheliumfree pages 6-9, wells2005fatiguecrackgrowth pages 6-9, wells2005fatiguecrackgrowth pages 9-13, kim2022metallicmaterialevaluation pages 4-5, adams2022cryogenicacceleratedfatigue pages 4-7, kim2022metallicmaterialevaluation pages 5-9)

info.query: What equipment and facilities are used for cryogenic mechanical testing of metals (tension, fracture toughness, fatigue) at 77 K, 20 K and 4 K? Cover liquid-nitrogen and liquid-helium immersion cryostats, cold-gas flow-through environmental chambers, cryocooler (Gifford-McMahon or pulse-tube) conduction-cooled rigs that need no liquid helium, and testing in liquid hydrogen; strain measurement and extensometry at cryogenic temperature; the commercial makers named in methods sections (load frames, cryostats, cryocoolers); the main documented test facilities (national labs, NASA centers, magnet labs, CERN, KIT, NIMS) with their temperature ranges; and cost, helium use and throughput where reported. Give citations and DOIs.
